stem: Briefly describe the structure of the Brain
solution:
The brain is the central information processing organ of the body. It is protected by the **skull** and covered by **cranial meninges**, and is divided into **forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain**.

1. **Meninges:** an outer **dura mater**, a very thin middle **arachnoid** and an inner **pia mater** in contact with the brain tissue.
2. **Forebrain:** consists of **cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus**.
   - The **cerebrum** forms the major part of the brain. A deep cleft divides it into the left and right **cerebral hemispheres**, connected by the **corpus callosum**. The outer **cerebral cortex** (grey matter) is thrown into folds and contains motor, sensory and association areas; the inner myelinated fibre tracts form the **white matter**.
   - The **thalamus**, around which the cerebrum wraps, is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.
   - The **hypothalamus** lies at the base of the thalamus; it controls body temperature, eating and drinking and secretes hypothalamic hormones.
   - The inner parts of the hemispheres with amygdala, hippocampus, etc., form the **limbic system**.
3. **Midbrain:** lies between the thalamus/hypothalamus and the pons. The **cerebral aqueduct** passes through it; its dorsal part has four round swellings, the **corpora quadrigemina**.
4. **Hindbrain:** comprises **pons** (fibre tracts interconnecting brain regions), **cerebellum** (very convoluted surface) and **medulla oblongata** (centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions), which is connected to the spinal cord.
5. Midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata together form the **brain stem**, which connects the brain and the spinal cord.
groundedIn: §18.4; §18.4.1; §18.4.2; §18.4.3; Fig. 18.4 — skull and cranial meninges (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater); three major parts; cerebrum, hemispheres, corpus callosum, cortex, white matter, thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system; cerebral aqueduct, corpora quadrigemina; pons, cerebellum, medulla; brain stem

stem: Central neural system (CNS) and Peripheral neural system (PNS)
solution:
| Basis of comparison | Central neural system (CNS) | Peripheral neural system (PNS) |
|---|---|---|
| Components | **Brain and spinal cord** | **All the nerves of the body** associated with the brain and spinal cord (cranial and spinal nerves) |
| Function | **Site of information processing and control** | Carries impulses between the tissues/organs and the CNS |
| Fibres | Contains the processing centres; fibre tracts form its white matter | Has **afferent fibres** (tissues/organs to CNS) and **efferent fibres** (CNS to tissues/organs) |
| Divisions | Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord | **Somatic neural system** and **autonomic neural system** (sympathetic and parasympathetic) |
| Protection | Brain protected by the skull and covered by cranial meninges | No such bony covering |
groundedIn: §18.2; §18.4; §18.4.1; §18.3 — CNS includes brain and spinal cord, site of information processing and control; PNS comprises all nerves associated with the CNS, afferent and efferent fibres, somatic and autonomic divisions; brain protected by skull and meninges; myelinated fibres found in spinal and cranial nerves

solution:
| Basis of comparison | Resting potential | Action potential |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Electrical potential difference across the **resting** plasma membrane | Electrical potential difference across the membrane at the **stimulated** site; it is the **nerve impulse** |
| State of membrane | **Polarised** | **Depolarised** (polarity reversed) |
| Charge | Outer surface **positive**, inner surface **negative** | Outer surface **negative**, inner surface **positive** |
| Permeability | More permeable to \(\text{K}^+\), nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\) | Membrane becomes freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\), with rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) |
| Maintained / caused by | Ionic gradients maintained by the **sodium-potassium pump** (3 \(\text{Na}^+\) out for 2 \(\text{K}^+\) in) | A **stimulus** applied to the polarised membrane |
| Duration | Persists while the neuron is not conducting an impulse | Extremely short-lived; \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses out and restores the resting potential |
groundedIn: §18.3.1; Fig. 18.2 — resting membrane more permeable to K+, nearly impermeable to Na+; sodium-potassium pump 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in; outer positive inner negative, polarised, resting potential; stimulus makes membrane freely permeable to Na+, polarity reversed, action potential is the nerve impulse; short-lived, K+ restores resting potential

stem: Polarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre
solution:
A resting nerve fibre has a **polarised membrane**: its outer surface is positively charged and its inner surface negatively charged.

1. The neural membrane has **ion channels** that are selectively permeable to different ions.
2. At rest, the axonal membrane is comparatively **more permeable to \(\text{K}^+\)** and **nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\)**; it is also impermeable to the **negatively charged proteins** of the axoplasm.
3. So the **axoplasm** contains a high concentration of \(\text{K}^+\) and negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of \(\text{Na}^+\), while the **fluid outside** has a low concentration of \(\text{K}^+\) and a high concentration of \(\text{Na}^+\). This forms a concentration gradient.
4. These ionic gradients are maintained by the **sodium-potassium pump**, which actively transports **3 \(\text{Na}^+\) outwards for 2 \(\text{K}^+\) into the cell**.
5. As a result the outer surface becomes positive and the inner surface negative, i.e., the membrane is **polarised**. The potential difference across it is the **resting potential**.
groundedIn: §18.3.1 — ion channels selectively permeable; resting membrane more permeable to K+, nearly impermeable to Na+ and impermeable to negatively charged proteins; concentration gradient; sodium-potassium pump 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in; outer surface positive, inner negative, polarised; resting potential

stem: Depolarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre
solution:
**Depolarisation** is the reversal of the polarity of the nerve fibre membrane at the site of a stimulus.

1. When a **stimulus** is applied at a site (say A) on the polarised membrane, the membrane at A becomes **freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\)**.
2. This causes a **rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\)**, which reverses the polarity: the **outer surface becomes negative** and the **inner surface positive**. The membrane at A is now **depolarised**.
3. The potential difference across the membrane at A is the **action potential**, i.e., the **nerve impulse**.
4. Just ahead (site B) the membrane is still positive outside and negative inside, so current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A. The polarity at B is reversed and an action potential is generated there. Repeated along the axon, this conducts the impulse.
5. The rise in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is extremely short-lived and is followed by a rise in \(\text{K}^+\) permeability; \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses out and the **resting potential is restored** (repolarisation), making the fibre responsive to further stimulation.
groundedIn: §18.3.1; Fig. 18.2 — stimulus at site A makes membrane freely permeable to Na+, rapid influx, polarity reversed, depolarised; action potential is the nerve impulse; current flow from A to B and conduction along the axon; short-lived, K+ diffuses out and restores the resting potential

stem: Transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse
solution:
At a **chemical synapse** the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are separated by a fluid-filled **synaptic cleft**, and the impulse is carried across it by chemicals called **neurotransmitters**.

1. The **axon terminals** of the pre-synaptic neuron contain **synaptic vesicles** filled with neurotransmitters.
2. When an impulse (action potential) arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the membrane.
3. The vesicles **fuse with the plasma membrane** and **release their neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft**.
4. The neurotransmitters **bind to their specific receptors** on the **post-synaptic membrane**.
5. This binding **opens ion channels**, allowing the entry of ions, which can generate a **new potential** in the post-synaptic neuron.
6. The new potential may be either **excitatory** or **inhibitory**.
groundedIn: §18.3.2; Fig. 18.3 — chemical synapse with fluid-filled synaptic cleft; vesicles with neurotransmitters in axon terminals; impulse stimulates vesicles to fuse with membrane and release neurotransmitters; binding to receptors on post-synaptic membrane opens ion channels; new potential excitatory or inhibitory

context: Draw labelled diagrams of the following:
solution:
Draw a myelinated multipolar neuron (book figure attached).

**Labels a marker looks for:** dendrites, Nissl's granules, cell body, nucleus, Schwann cell, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon terminal, synaptic knob.

- **Cell body** at the top, with a central **nucleus** and cytoplasm dotted with **Nissl's granules**.
- Several short, repeatedly branched **dendrites** projecting from the cell body.
- One long **axon** leaving the cell body, wrapped by **Schwann cells** that form the **myelin sheath**; the gaps between adjacent sheaths are the **nodes of Ranvier**.
- The distal end of the axon is branched into **axon terminals**, each ending in a bulb-like **synaptic knob**.

The book's figure labels the Schwann cell as 'Schwan cell'.
groundedIn: §18.3; Fig. 18.1 — cell body with Nissl's granules, dendrites, axon with branched distal end ending in synaptic knobs; Schwann cells form myelin sheath; nodes of Ranvier

context: Draw labelled diagrams of the following:
solution:
Draw the sagittal section of the human brain (book figure attached).

**Labels a marker looks for:** cerebrum, cerebral hemisphere, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus (bracketed together as **forebrain**), midbrain, cerebral aqueduct, pons, cerebellum, medulla (bracketed together as **hindbrain**), spinal cord.

- The large, folded **cerebrum** occupies the top and front, with the arched **corpus callosum** inside it.
- The **thalamus** lies below the corpus callosum, with the **hypothalamus** at its base.
- The **midbrain** lies below the thalamus/hypothalamus, with the **cerebral aqueduct** running through it.
- Below and behind are the **pons** (front), the highly convoluted **cerebellum** (behind) and the **medulla**, which continues down as the **spinal cord**.

context: Write short notes on the following:
solution:
**Coordination** is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another. The **neural system** and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and integrate the activities of all organs so that they function in a synchronised fashion.

1. The neural system provides an **organised network of point-to-point connections** for **quick coordination**.
2. It is made of **neurons**, highly specialised cells that **detect, receive and transmit** different kinds of stimuli.
3. It coordinates and integrates functions as well as the metabolic and homeostatic activities of all the organs, helping maintain **homeostasis**.
4. **Example:** during physical exercise, the increased energy and oxygen demand of muscles is met by an increase in the rate of respiration, heart beat and blood flow; when exercise stops, nerves, lungs, heart and kidney gradually return to normal. The functions of muscles, lungs, heart, blood vessels and kidney are thus coordinated.
5. Neural coordination works through **transmission of nerve impulses** along neurons and **impulse conduction across synapses**.
groundedIn: §18.0; §18.1 — coordination defined; neural and endocrine systems jointly coordinate; point-to-point connections for quick coordination; exercise example; neurons detect, receive and transmit stimuli; coordinates metabolic and homeostatic activities (stated in the chapter Summary)

context: Write short notes on the following:
solution:
The **forebrain** consists of the **cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus**.

1. **Cerebrum:** forms the major part of the human brain. A deep cleft divides it into the **left and right cerebral hemispheres**, connected by a tract of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**.
2. **Cerebral cortex:** the outer layer of cells, thrown into prominent folds; called **grey matter** because neuron cell bodies are concentrated here. It contains **motor areas, sensory areas** and **association areas** (responsible for intersensory associations, memory and communication).
3. **White matter:** the inner part of the hemispheres, formed by myelinated fibre tracts.
4. **Thalamus:** wrapped by the cerebrum; a major coordinating centre for **sensory and motor signalling**.
5. **Hypothalamus:** lies at the base of the thalamus; has centres controlling **body temperature, eating and drinking**, and neurosecretory cells that secrete **hypothalamic hormones**.
6. **Limbic system:** the inner parts of the hemispheres with amygdala, hippocampus, etc.; with the hypothalamus it regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.
groundedIn: §18.4.1; Fig. 18.4 — forebrain consists of cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus; hemispheres and corpus callosum; cerebral cortex grey matter with motor, sensory and association areas; white matter; thalamus as sensory and motor coordinating centre; hypothalamus centres and hormones; limbic system

context: Write short notes on the following:
solution:
The **midbrain** is the middle part of the brain.

1. **Position:** located between the **thalamus/hypothalamus** of the forebrain and the **pons** of the hindbrain.
2. A canal called the **cerebral aqueduct** passes through it.
3. Its dorsal portion consists mainly of four round swellings (lobes) called the **corpora quadrigemina**.
4. **Function:** it receives and integrates **visual, tactile and auditory inputs**.
5. With the pons and medulla oblongata it forms the **brain stem**, which connects the brain and the spinal cord.
groundedIn: §18.4.2; §18.4.3; Fig. 18.4 — midbrain between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; cerebral aqueduct; corpora quadrigemina; part of brain stem; receives and integrates visual, tactile and auditory inputs (stated in the chapter Summary)

context: Write short notes on the following:
solution:
The **hindbrain** comprises the **pons, cerebellum and medulla** (medulla oblongata).

1. **Pons:** consists of **fibre tracts** that interconnect different regions of the brain.
2. **Cerebellum:** has a **very convoluted surface** to provide additional space for many more neurons; it integrates information received from the **semicircular canals of the ear** and the auditory system.
3. **Medulla oblongata:** connected to the **spinal cord**; contains centres that control **respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions**.
4. The pons and medulla, together with the midbrain, form the **brain stem**, which connects the brain and the spinal cord.
groundedIn: §18.4.3; Fig. 18.4 — hindbrain comprises pons, cerebellum, medulla; pons fibre tracts; cerebellum convoluted surface for more neurons; medulla connected to spinal cord with respiratory, cardiovascular and gastric centres; brain stem; cerebellum integrates information from semicircular canals and auditory system (stated in the chapter Summary)

context: Write short notes on the following:
solution:
A **synapse** is a junction through which a nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another. It is formed by the membranes of a **pre-synaptic neuron** and a **post-synaptic neuron**, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the **synaptic cleft**.

There are two types:

1. **Electrical synapse:** the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are in very close proximity and electrical current flows directly from one neuron into the other. Transmission is similar to conduction along a single axon and is **always faster** than across a chemical synapse. Electrical synapses are **rare** in our system.
2. **Chemical synapse:** the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft. An impulse arriving at the axon terminal makes the **synaptic vesicles** fuse with the membrane and release **neurotransmitters** into the cleft. These bind to **receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane, open ion channels and generate a new potential that may be **excitatory or inhibitory**.
groundedIn: §18.3.2; Fig. 18.3 — synapse formed by pre- and post-synaptic membranes, may or may not be separated by synaptic cleft; electrical synapses close proximity, faster, rare; chemical synapse with neurotransmitters, receptors, ion channels, excitatory or inhibitory potential

stem: Give a brief account of Mechanism of synaptic transmission.
solution:
A nerve impulse passes from one neuron to the next across a **synapse**, formed by the membranes of a **pre-synaptic** and a **post-synaptic neuron**.

**At an electrical synapse:** the two membranes are in very close proximity, and electrical current flows **directly** from one neuron into the other. Transmission is very similar to conduction along a single axon and is always faster than at a chemical synapse. Such synapses are rare in our system.

**At a chemical synapse:** the two membranes are separated by a fluid-filled **synaptic cleft**, and **neurotransmitters** carry the impulse across it.

1. The **axon terminals** contain **synaptic vesicles** filled with neurotransmitters.
2. The arriving **action potential** stimulates the vesicles to move towards the plasma membrane.
3. The vesicles **fuse** with the membrane and **release neurotransmitters** into the synaptic cleft.
4. The neurotransmitters **bind to specific receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane.
5. The binding **opens ion channels**, letting ions enter and generating a **new potential** in the post-synaptic neuron.
6. This new potential may be **excitatory** or **inhibitory**.
groundedIn: §18.3.2; Fig. 18.3 — synapse of pre- and post-synaptic membranes; electrical synapse direct current flow, faster, rare; chemical synapse with synaptic cleft; vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitters; receptors on post-synaptic membrane; ion channels open; excitatory or inhibitory potential

stem: Explain the role of \(\text{Na}^+\) in the generation of action potential.
solution:
The **action potential** is generated by a sudden **influx of \(\text{Na}^+\)** that reverses the polarity of the membrane.

1. **At rest:** the axonal membrane is nearly **impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\)**. The fluid outside has a **high \(\text{Na}^+\)** concentration and the axoplasm a low one; the **sodium-potassium pump** maintains this by transporting 3 \(\text{Na}^+\) outwards for 2 \(\text{K}^+\) inwards. The outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative (polarised, resting potential).
2. **On stimulation:** the membrane at the stimulated site becomes **freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\)**.
3. \(\text{Na}^+\) rushes in (**rapid influx**) along its concentration gradient, so the **inner surface becomes positive** and the **outer surface negative**. The membrane is **depolarised**.
4. The potential difference at this site is the **action potential**, i.e., the nerve impulse.
5. Current then flows to the adjacent polarised site, where \(\text{Na}^+\) entry again reverses polarity, so the impulse is conducted along the axon.
6. The rise in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is **extremely short-lived**; it is followed by a rise in \(\text{K}^+\) permeability, \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses out and the resting potential is restored.
groundedIn: §18.3.1; Fig. 18.2 — resting membrane nearly impermeable to Na+, high Na+ outside, sodium-potassium pump; stimulus makes membrane freely permeable to Na+, rapid influx, polarity reversed, action potential; conduction to site B; Na+ permeability short-lived, K+ restores resting potential

solution:
| Basis of difference | Myelinated axon | Non-myelinated axon |
|---|---|---|
| Covering | Enveloped by **Schwann cells** that form a **myelin sheath** around the axon | Enclosed by a Schwann cell that **does not form a myelin sheath** |
| Nodes of Ranvier | Present: gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths | Absent |
| Occurrence | **Spinal and cranial nerves** | **Autonomous and somatic neural systems** |

stem: Which part of the human brain is the most developed?
solution: The **cerebrum** (part of the forebrain). It forms the **major part of the human brain**; its cerebral cortex is thrown into prominent folds and contains motor, sensory and association areas for complex functions like memory and communication.
groundedIn: §18.4.1 — cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain; cortex thrown into prominent folds with motor, sensory and association areas

stem: Which part of our central neural system acts as a master clock?
solution: The **hypothalamus**. Its **suprachiasmatic nucleus** acts as the master clock that regulates the **circadian (24-hour) rhythms** of the body, such as the sleep-wake cycle. The hypothalamus also controls body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking.
groundedIn: §18.4; §18.4.1 — brain controls circadian (24-hour) rhythms; hypothalamus centres control body temperature, eating and drinking; BEYOND CHAPTER: the hypothalamus (its suprachiasmatic nucleus) is the master clock of circadian rhythms, e.g. the sleep-wake cycle

stem: impulse conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre and unmyelinated nerve fibre
solution:
| Basis of difference | Myelinated nerve fibre | Unmyelinated nerve fibre |
|---|---|---|
| Covering | Myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells, interrupted at **nodes of Ranvier** | Enclosed by a Schwann cell with **no myelin sheath** |
| Site of depolarisation | Only at the **nodes of Ranvier** | Along the **whole length** of the axon membrane, site after site (A to B and onwards) |
| Mode of conduction | **Saltatory**: the impulse jumps from node to node | **Continuous**: the impulse moves step by step along the membrane |
| Speed | **Faster** | **Slower** |
| Energy use | Less, as ion exchange is limited to the nodes | More, as ion exchange occurs along the whole membrane |
groundedIn: §18.3; §18.3.1; Fig. 18.2 — myelin sheath of Schwann cells with nodes of Ranvier; unmyelinated fibre without myelin sheath; impulse generated at site A arrives at site B and the sequence is repeated along the axon; BEYOND CHAPTER: saltatory conduction with depolarisation only at nodes of Ranvier, faster conduction and lower energy use in myelinated fibres
